items.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023
items.q: my concept of this record had to do with modern ancestors, okay, not the Sojourner Truths but the John Coltranes and the Miles Davises and the Nina Simones, okay, and the Carmen McRaes and so forth and so on.

ctx.x: This is, you know jazz is such a wonderful experiment where we’re exploring possibilities all the time. It’s the nature of the music you know. And I’m young and I’m anxious and I’m learning and I want to be liked, I want to be known and recognized for being a musician not just a singer myself you see and that little arranging part, there’s something so wonderful and diplomatic and democratic about the experience of this music and to stay open to the possibilities. And you think you might be on this certain track…

about singers yet, okay? We haven’t even talked about the Ellas and the Sarahs and the Carmen McRaes and the Bettys and all that. Okay? This is just how the music — I think I was a sponge, I think I still am. I was just absorbing from the masterful, from the masters really, of that time. I’m in my early twenties and they are fully realized artists at that time in their careers. And I’m just really taking whatever they offer and happy to be in the mix.

Do you think there’s a difference — well there’s a difference sometimes between instrumentalists and vocalists — but I frequently ask the question of practicing jazz musicians now if there are wrong notes in improvising. And almost all of them say no, like emphatically. And then they may go on and explain, well let me tell you why. But so my question is if Miles Davis played a note that sort of perks up your ear and you go like why did he choose that but he gets away with it, does a singer have the same liberty…
